title: Pros, cons of commission-based retirement accounts
description: Barron's Associate Publisher Jack Otter on Merrill Lynch reportedly considering ending a ban on commission-based retirement accounts and the risks of investing in hot sectors.

asr.full_text: Our colleagues and friends at the Wall Street Journal, on the day that the Dow is diving, have an interesting report that Merrill Lynch might consider reversing a ban on commissions for those who handle retirement accounts. That's a Barron's associate publisher, great author, Jack Otter. Jack, what does this mean, can you explain? Sure. First, let's get the bad news out of the way. When someone has a commission that is a financial incentive to sell you something as a lot of salesmen do they're going to try to sell you stuff when it comes to investing that's not always a good idea they should be selling you only things that are absolutely the best for Neil Cavuto whoever their client is so Commission's are dangerous most people in this business are good an honest only do the right thing but the law of numbers says some people going to go in there and pushing things products that So, what do you think are the possibilities if you were to get back at people, they would be really hurt, right? No, commissions are dangerous. No. Commissioners are dangerous. Most people in this business are good and honest and will only do the right thing, but the law of numbers says some people are going to go in there and pushing things, products that their clients shouldn't have. So, in the Obama administration, the Department of Labor came up with a standard called a fiduciary standard. Right. Just as doctors take the Hippocratic oath, lawyers have an oath financial advisers on retirement and that rule was problematic for a lot of reasons we won't go into it was basically iced in March it looks like it's dead and so Merrill is going back to this idea of commissions and I will say that the rule was problematic for a number of reasons, one of which is if you, let's say, you've got, I don't know, a million bucks in your 401K. You've saved diligently for 30 years, and now you're maybe thinking about retirement. You go to an advisor. Well, if they're not charging commissions, they've got to charge you somehow. And the standard thing to do is to charge you a percentage of assets. So 1% of a million bucks is 10 grand. Well, it might be worth it for one year to pay that and get a great financial plan and everything else, but $10,000 every single year, are you really getting your money's worth there. A commission based plan would probably save you money, in the end. So I can see both sides of it. Why do they need it now? These guys have been making money hand over fist. It's not as if they sorely need it. What they would tell you is that with the smaller clients, they don't have a good way, a good financial arrangement, so that everybody— you know, the broker makes a little bit of money and the client still gets good service. I think one of the better ways to go about this is an hourly fee. If people don't like writing a check, they'd rather not see it. But I think that for small clients with fairly simple needs, I think actually that is the best approach Did they still avoid selling you something you don't need like Annuities someone doesn't really want annuities they keep forcing into annuities Would this new thing allow them to do that It would allow them to do that Now two things One the result of this law is The annuity business itself has gotten a little bit better. Frankly no, you're not, especially because the reason that this sector is so on fire is disruption. AT&T isn't buying companies media companies because hey they want to go to Hollywood it's because they're worried about what the future brings. So do you recommend of course I mean you'd be richly rewarded for just buying technology and all that. The last few years where the Nasdaq 100 what have you. So you don't have to go out and buy the stocks you already own them in a a diversified portfolio and frankly any more than 15% of five stocks is a little bit scary.
